articles.title: Active Lubrication Brakes in Tabletop and Hand-Held Haptic Surgical Drilling Simulators
articles.content: Haptic user interfaces that provide both kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback have strong potential to enhance a wide range of medical training simulations. Yet, designing such devices remains challenging due to constraints related to integration, workspace, cost, and the need for diverse feedback types. To address these issues, we investigated the applicability of a novel type of brake based on the active lubrication principle. This actuator is compact, low-cost, and able to deliver both kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback. To demonstrate its advantages, we focused on maxillofacial drilling in surgical training. We designed, implemented and evaluated a one-degree-of-freedom drill mock-up embedded into a tabletop prototype able to render axial forces up to 4.5 N. To assess both the relevance of combined feedback and the suitability of this actuator for surgical simulation, we conducted two studies: one with fourteen non-surgeon participants and another with six maxillofacial surgeons. Results confirm the potential of this actuation approach for surgery simulators and highlighted the importance of combined kinesthetic and vibrotactile feedback to improve realism, user preference, and task performance. Based on the surgeons’ feedback, we then proposed a redesigned brake, with an improved control method, implemented in a new hand-held version of a drill replica. Preliminary characterisation shows that the new prototype can render forces up to 5.5 N and produce higher vibration amplitudes than the initial design.

articles.title: Reconciling Reduced the Sense of Ownership and Agency Toward a Virtual Keypad With Enhanced Haptic Experience Using Visually Adjusted Self-Haptics for Key-Input Interaction
articles.content: Self-Haptics is a tactile feedback technique where users utilize their own body to generate tactile sensations. This method allows the body to act purely as a prop, making it useful for virtual objects and user interfaces not directly related to the body. However, any method for maintaining the sense of ownership (SoO) and agency (SoA) of the user’s body and interaction targets that aligns with the perceptual interaction by visual cues has not been established. To address this, we present the concept of “(Not My) Self-Haptics,” which aims to resolve these inconsistencies, leveraging vision’s dominance in sensory integration. In this study, through the user’s interaction with a virtual keypad (VPad) displayed at the position of the real hand (RHand), we clarified how the user’s experience changed, including SoO and SoA toward the VPad, and how the task performance was affected by the interaction with the VPad. The results show that displaying the VHand at a misaligned position with the RHand or hiding the VHand significantly reduces SoO and SoA toward the VPad. Conversely, obtaining tactile feedback through Self-Haptics during interaction with the VPad significantly decreases task performance and increases SoO toward the VPad displayed near the VHand. Despite these unintended effects, this visual modification also significantly enhances Autotelics, Involvement, and Realism based on the Haptic Experience Inventory compared to typical mid-air interaction without tactile feedback. These findings contribute to the understanding of the interaction between visual and tactile sensations in Self-Haptics and the feasibility and practicality of “(Not My) Self-Haptics”.

articles.title: VibGrasp: Spatiotemporal Vibration Based Multimodal Haptic Rendering With a Lightweight Exo-Glove for 3D Shape Perception
articles.content: Haptic feedback has been employed to enhance shape perception during grasp interactions, improving immersion and task performance in extended reality (XR). Although wearable devices offer precise multi-phalangeal haptic feedback, their bulkiness and complexity often hinder practicality. In addition, fingertip-based tactile feedback often limits users’ ability to perceive a continuous and sequential sensation across the finger surfaces during power grasp. We present VibGrasp, a haptic shape-rendering method and a supporting haptic glove that synchronizes spatiotemporal vibrotactile feedback across multiple phalanges with 1-DOF kinesthetic feedback. Using the funneling illusion and duration-modulated vibration patterns, our approach delivers sequential, continuous sensations along the finger to render various shapes. We also develop a lightweight exoskeleton glove with two dorsal-mounted vibration actuators designed to transmit feedback to the ventral surfaces without obstructing motion. Two perception studies demonstrated consistent shape associations and clear preferences for specific patterns. A VR user-experience study further showed that VibGrasp achieved higher ratings for realism, satisfaction, and harmony than prior approaches. These findings offer insights into improving immersive and efficient haptic shape rendering in XR.

articles.title: Propeller-Based Handheld Force-Feedback Device for Navigation
articles.content: This article presents an evaluation of CrazyJoystick, a propeller-based handheld force-feedback device, for spatial navigation tasks in real-world and virtual reality environments. Building upon prior work validating the device's on-demand aerial deployment and directional cue discriminability, we investigated whether propeller-based kinesthetic torque cues can support effective wayfinding during continuous locomotion. We developed navigation-specific algorithms that generate egocentric directional cues using hierarchical decision logic optimized for dynamic heading corrections. Two user studies (N = 12) compared CrazyJoystick with vibrotactile baselines. Study 1 evaluated multi-waypoint navigation through four path configurations in a real-world environment with visual occlusion; CrazyJoystick reduced completion time by 54.6% and path deviation by 25.8% relative to vibrotactile guidance. Study 2 assessed target localization in a VR treasure hunt with minimal lighting; CrazyJoystick enabled 43.2% faster completion and 79% higher walking speeds. Both studies revealed consistent workload reductions. These findings demonstrate that propeller-based kinesthetic feedback supports efficient navigation during sustained locomotion, establishing propeller-based torque directional cues as a viable alternative to vibrotactile encoding for dynamic wayfinding tasks.

articles.title: A Wearable Shoulder Skin-Deformation Device Generating Illusory Forces for Posture Correction
articles.content: The hanger reflex is a haptic illusion in which skin-shear deformation elicits a directional force sensation. This study presents a wearable haptic device that uses four pneumatic airbags to apply controlled skin shear to both shoulders for posture guidance. Although previous work has shown that shoulder skin shear can induce illusory forces, neither the magnitude of these forces nor their influence on upper-body posture has been quantitatively examined. In Experiment 1, we quantified perceived force using a psychophysical comparison between skin-shear stimulation and real traction forces. The device generated perceived forces of up to 4.4 N in the forward direction and 4.8 N in the backward direction, more than an order of magnitude larger than those reported for conventional illusion-based haptic methods. Perceived force increased systematically with air pressure and was well approximated by a linear model. In Experiment 2, we evaluated the effects of these stimuli on upper-body posture by measuring trunk pitch under varying initial postures, stimulation directions, and intensities. The device induced consistent posture adjustments, particularly in the backward direction, with significant effects of both initial posture and stimulus intensity. These results demonstrate that shoulder hanger-reflex stimulation provides strong, controllable force sensations and measurable posture modification, supporting its use in wearable posture-support and rehabilitation systems.

articles.title: Sensitivity at the Edges of the Finger Enables Mixed Reality Force Feedback
articles.content: We introduce a new paradigm for rendering high-force sensations by stimulating the edges of the fingerpad rather than the central contact surface. This non-blocking approach preserves natural finger use, enabling simultaneous physical and virtual interactions. To investigate its feasibility, we proposed a mechanotransduction mechanism and conducted biomechanical and psychophysical studies. Our results show that the fingerpad edges are nearly as sensitive as the center under low forces, become roughly 117% more sensitive under moderate forces, and maintain sensitivity at higher forces. The edges also exhibit increased stiffness and tolerate higher forces before discomfort. Furthermore, the left edge exhibited approximately 143% higher sensitivity than the right edge in the right hand. Using these insights, we built a compact wearable device that provides multi-DOF force feedback without blocking the fingerpad and demonstrated its use in VR/AR scenarios. These findings support edge-based stimulation as a viable approach for high-force, scalable haptic feedback in mixed reality and teleoperation systems.

articles.title: ThermalTexture: Temperature-Integrated Surface Rendering Using Thermal Referral Induced by Texture Slip-Feedback
articles.content: Thermal–vibration feedback has been reported to elicit the thermal referral phenomenon, offering new possibilities for enhancing user experience. Yet, little research has explored whether thermal referral occurs in the presence of texture-slip feedback. To address this, we developed a custom haptic device capable of delivering integrated thermal and slip feedback to the middle and distal phalanges of an index finger. We primarily estimated the thermal referral occurrence under passive and active touch conditions across two different perceptual experiments, while each further examined its impact on texture perceptions and user experiences (UX). In Perceptual Experiment 1 (passive), we observed the highest occurrence of thermal referral at 40 $^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ (0.86 on a 0–1 scale), and found that referral increased the median of perceived roughness from 43.5 to 60 on a 0—100 scale. In Perceptual Experiment 2 (active), the kinesthetic cues significantly enhanced thermal referral, with the occurrence probability at 24 $^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ increasing to 0.86 compared to 0.51 (0—1 scale) in the first study. In addition, high UX ratings demonstrated the applicability of our device to temperature-integrated virtual texture interactions. Our findings expand the scope of thermal referral and highlight the potential for enabling VR users to interact with virtual surfaces that provide temperature cues.

articles.title: Beyond Mean Pooling: Statistical Meta-Aggregation for Subject-Level EEG Classification in Parkinson's Disease
articles.content: Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive, temporally precise tool for studying neural alterations associated with Parkinson's disease (PD). When labels are defined at the subject level but inputs are epoch level, a key design choice is how epoch-wise predictions are aggregated to a single subject-level decision. Most prior work uses mean pooling, which assumes all epochs contribute equally and independently. This study proposes a statistical meta-aggregation strategy that represents each subject by 14 descriptors of the epoch-wise prediction distribution, including measures of central tendency, dispersion, shape, and high-confidence concentration. Using a self-supervised contrastive encoder trained on task-evoked EEG from the Simon conflict task, and a sample of 90 subjects including 57 PD and 33 control, this work evaluates the proposed framework under subject-wise five-fold cross-validation. Replacing mean pooling with statistical meta-aggregation lifts subject-level ROC-AUC from 0.655 to 0.872 for logistic regression and from 0.724 to 0.840 for support vector machines, without modifying the encoder or the classifier family. Averaging predictions across three independent self-supervised pretraining seeds yields competitive performance and improved balanced accuracy. These results suggest that, in this dataset, the way epoch-level predictions are summarized at the subject level has a substantial effect on final PD classification performance.
articles.author: Taghipour Langrodi, P., Khodadadi, A., Rezaei, F., Anvarian, Z., Sotero, R. C., Madadi, S.

articles.title: Optimising neural contrast and minimising tissue shrinkage in dragon lizard brains: buffered Lugol's iodine versus phosphotungstic acid for contrast-enhanced μCT
articles.content: Contrast-enhanced micro-computed tomography (CT) has become a valuable tool for addressing neuroanatomical questions that previously required destructive histology. As a relatively new technique, it remains subject to ongoing technical refinement, and taxon- and tissue-specific protocol optimisation. We evaluated the performance of two common contrast-enhancing agents, buffered Lugol's iodine and phosphotungstic acid (PTA) in aqueous solution, for CT visualisation of the nervous system in the Jacky dragon lizard, Amphibolurus muricatus by comparing staining time, contrast specificity and brain tissue shrinkage evaluated at three concentrations (1.25%, 2.5% and 5%). Buffered Lugol's iodine outperformed aqueous PTA by requiring shorter staining times (as short as four days) and providing better white matter-grey matter differentiation, whereas PTA required longer incubation periods of approximately three weeks and produced poorer white-grey matter differentiation. Importantly, buffered Lugol's iodine produced higher brain-to-endocast occupancy estimates than aqueous PTA, suggesting substantially reduced tissue shrinkage. PTA-treated specimens exhibited an estimated 13.3% reduction in occupancy and approximately 20% greater brain tissue shrinkage than buffered Lugol's-treated specimens. Together, these findings demonstrate that buffered Lugol's iodine staining provides the high level of internal tissue contrast required to resolve fine-scale neuroanatomical organisation in three dimensions, preserves the spatial relationships among anatomical structures, and reduces artefacts, all of which result in a closer correspondence between the brain and endocranial cavity. From a practical perspective, the study provides guidance for contrast agent selection in future CT studies and reveals that buffered Lugol's iodine is better suited to fine-scale neuroanatomical, volumetric and geometric morphometric analyses, whereas PTA is advantageous for applications prioritising general soft-tissue or musculoskeletal visualisation.
articles.author: Navea, F., Black, J. R., Dissanayake, D. S. B., Whiteley, S. L., Kerr, C. C., Collin, S. P., Crowe-Riddell, J. M.

articles.title: Enhancing cortical electrophysiological signatures of sleep overrides ER stress responses in sleep-deprived mice
articles.content: Sleep deprivation (SD) triggers characteristic changes in the cortical electroencephalogram (EEG) during waking and sleep, as well as upregulating molecular signatures of neuronal activity, synaptic plasticity, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress. This includes the induction of the unfolded protein response (UPR), the primary marker and adaptive mechanism of ER stress. Yet how cortical neuronal activity during SD contributes to the induction of these molecular signatures remains unknown. Here we investigate whether manipulating cortical activity during SD with a physiological stimulation paradigm (flickering light stimulation, FLS) affects the induction of the UPR. As expected, SD alone upregulated activity-dependent and UPR-related genes in cortex and led to increased EEG slow-wave activity (SWA) during subsequent NREM sleep, an electrophysiological signature of sleep need. Delivering FLS during SD, however, prevented the upregulation of activity- and UPR-related genes while inducing an additional increase in SWA during subsequent sleep. Further analysis of neuronal firing revealed that FLS induced brief neuronal silent (OFF) periods in awake animals during stimulation, thereby shifting cortical activity towards a brain state resembling sleep. These findings suggest that physiological manipulation of cortical activity during waking is sufficient to dissociate molecular signatures of ER stress from electrophysiological markers of sleep pressure. We propose that global sleep wake history and cortical network dynamics differentially regulate activity-dependent transcription and the accumulation of sleep pressure.

Safety of lecanemab in real-world patients with Alzheimer’s disease: a prospective, observational case series supported by FAERS signal analysis
articles.content: ObjectiveLecanemab, a humanized immunoglobulin monoclonal antibody, has been approved for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Although clinical trials have demonstrated its favorable safety profile, real-world studies are crucial for identifying rare adverse events (AEs) and evaluating post-marketing safety. This study aimed to evaluate the safety of lecanemab by combining a clinical prospective, observational case cohort with data from the FAERS database, thereby providing a robust basis for the identification of potential safety signals.MethodsA prospective and observational study was conducted on patients with mild-to-moderate AD receiving lecanemab treatment at a tertiary medical center in China from July 2024 to February 2026. Extracted data included demographic characteristics, time to onset of AEs, and clinical symptoms. Exposure-adjusted incidence rates were calculated per 100 patient-years (PYs). Disproportionality analysis was performed using the US Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), and safety signals for AEs observed in the cohort were evaluated utilizing reporting odds ratios (RORs) and proportional reporting ratios (PRRs). Additionally, data from these two real-world sources were compared and cross-validated.ResultsThe single-center prospective study enrolled a total of 91 patients. The median duration of lecanemab treatment was 185 days. Thirteen AEs were recorded (56.48/100 PYs), with the most frequent being amyloid-related imaging abnormalities-hemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H; defined as microhemorrhages and hemosiderin deposition) (12.39/100 PYs) and infusion-related reactions (IRRs) (8.85/100 PYs). In the FAERS database, the most frequently reported preferred terms (PTs) included headache, amyloid-related imaging abnormalities-edema/effusion (ARIA-E), ARIA-H, and IRRs. The majority of AEs occurred within the first 1–2 months after initiating lecanemab treatment (n = 393, 45.65%). Furthermore, FAERS analysis revealed a potential safety signal for cerebral infarction. However, this finding must be interpreted cautiously due to the lack of complete data on traditional stroke risk factors and concomitant antithrombotic use in spontaneous reports.ConclusionIn this single-center prospective observational study, lecanemab demonstrated a generally favorable safety profile. Patients with AD aged 65 to 85 years represent a high-risk demographic for AEs. Particular clinical vigilance is required regarding the occurrence of AEs within the first two months of lecanemab initiation. Notably, ARIA (including both ARIA-E and ARIA-H) can occur at any phase during the treatment course.
articles.author: Erhao Bao

articles.title: A systematic review of machine learning approaches for MRI-based brain tumor analysis
articles.content: Machine learning is now widely applied to magnetic resonance imaging-based brain tumor analysis, with task-specific performance metrics: the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) quantifies segmentation overlap, while the area under the curve (AUC) and accuracy measure classification performance. A PRISMA 2020 systematic review was conducted, searching Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore, and identified 213 eligible studies published between January 2018 and the final search date of March 16, 2026. Segmentation performance was synthesized by random-effects meta-analysis and classification performance was summarized descriptively. Classification, detection, and grading tasks dominated the literature, followed by segmentation; U-Net variants were the most frequent architectures, with transformer-based models growing fastest. The pooled mean DSC was 0.871 (95% CI: 0.852–0.889) with a 95% prediction interval of 0.7880.953, and heterogeneity was extreme (I2 = 99.9%), so the pooled mean should be read as a descriptive summary of the literature rather than a single underlying effect. The descriptive mean AUC across classification studies was 0.960. Methodological gaps were pervasive: only 18.8% of studies incorporated explainability, only 18.8% performed external validation, and none reported robustness metrics. Benchmark accuracy has outpaced clinical evidence: until models are validated on independent cohorts, evaluated for robustness under realistic acquisition shifts, and made interpretable to clinicians, reported performance is unlikely to translate into patient care.
articles.author: Almira Melsovna Kustubayeva

articles.title: Uncertainty-aware posture quality assessment with Bayesian liquid neural networks
articles.content: Automated posture quality assessment has become increasingly important in health and wellness technology. However, existing methods predominantly provide point estimates without quantifying prediction confidence, posing a critical limitation in safety-sensitive applications where incorrect assessments may lead to improper guidance. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a reliability-oriented evaluation framework based on Bayesian Liquid Neural Networks (LNNBI). Unlike conventional approaches, our method simultaneously delivers a quality score and a principled uncertainty measure derived from Bayesian variational inference. More importantly, we incorporate a rejection mechanism that enables the model to abstain from making predictions when uncertainty exceeds a predefined threshold, establishing a built-in safeguard for practical deployment. To support this framework, we construct a longitudinal dataset comprising 50 participants over 200 sessions, decomposing four fundamental human postures into seven biomechanical indicators. Experimental results demonstrate that LNNBI achieves 0.8715 accuracy and 0.9105 precision, outperforming LSTM, MC-GRU, TSGCN, and YoNet baselines. Uncertainty analysis reveals a strong correlation between prediction error and uncertainty (Pearson’s r = 0.73), confirming that the model reliably identifies its own low-confidence predictions. With a 15% rejection rate, the effective accuracy reaches 0.923. Correlation analysis further identifies Pelvic Position and Neutrality (r = 0.682) and Spinal Alignment (r = 0.595) as the most influential biomechanical indicators. This work offers a reliability-first perspective on automated posture assessment, with promising potential for deployment in personalized health coaching and remote guidance, particularly on GPU-accelerated systems.
articles.author: Zhi Tao

articles.title: Caudal optogenetic spinal stimulation promotes better therapeutic outcomes than rostral optogenetic stimulation following a cervical spinal cord injury
articles.content: PurposeSpinal stimulation, including optogenetic stimulation, is a promising therapeutic approach for promoting functional recovery after spinal cord injury (SCI). To date, most studies have delivered stimulation caudal to the level of the lesion. Therefore, there is a lack of understanding of how spinal stimulation rostral to the lesion may affect recovery. Here, we investigate the effects of optogenetic spinal stimulation rostral to the lesion site on forelimb functional recovery and axonal growth in a rat model of cervical SCI.MethodsFemale Long-Evans rats received a C4 hemicontusion, intraspinal injections of an optogenetic viral vector rostral to the injury site, and a micro-light-emitting diode (μLED) implant for optogenetic stimulation. Beginning 6 weeks post-injury, rats received 6 weeks of optogenetic or sham stimulation alongside forelimb reaching rehabilitation. Forelimb reaching success and growth-associated protein 43 (GAP43) percent area were compared with those in our previous study, which evaluated an identical paradigm, but with optogenetic stimulation positioned caudal to the injury.ResultsThe present results indicate that rostral stimulation did not enhance forelimb recovery on the forelimb reaching task and that forelimb reaching success was significantly higher in the caudal optogenetic stimulation group compared to the rostral stimulation group. Additionally, rostral stimulation did not enhance axonal growth within the cervical spinal cord compared with sham stimulation, whereas caudal optogenetic stimulation promoted significantly more axonal growth than rostral optogenetic stimulation.ConclusionOverall, these results indicate that caudal optogenetic stimulation promotes a greater therapeutic impact than rostral optogenetic stimulation.
